slide 6 ('Aggregating metrics across components'): [fact] The note recommends a “p99 across services” as percentile aggregation, but averaging component p99 values does not produce the system-wide p99 experienced by users. Fix: Explain that end-to-end percentiles should be computed from correlated request-level measurements or a suitable latency-distribution model; component p99 values may be shown separately but should not be averaged into a system p99. (found before the rewrite; the slide may have moved)

slide 7 ('Scenario 1: Microservice deployment walkthrough'): [fact] The automatic rollback rule is misstated: exceeding the error budget is not itself a rollback trigger, because an exhausted budget indicates that the budget has already been consumed rather than that the current deployment has breached it. Fix: Say to roll back when the new version breaches a defined SLO or short-window burn-rate threshold, and to stop releases when the remaining error budget is insufficient. (rewritten to fix this; not re-read by the reviewer)

slide 9 ('Evaluating supplied project metrics step‑by‑step'): [code] The scorecard divides by len(entries) without handling an empty service log, and its budget calculation can divide by zero when an SLO permits no errors. Fix: Skip or explicitly report services with no observations, validate that max_error is positive, and define the budget calculation using the SLO’s permitted bad-event rate and the measured bad-event rate. (rewritten to fix this; not re-read by the reviewer)

slide 9 ('Evaluating supplied project metrics step‑by‑step'): [fact] The slide does not define the observation window, request denominator, or incident semantics needed to interpret the computed error rate, MTBF, and MTTR reproducibly. Fix: State that error rate uses failed requests divided by all valid requests in a defined window, MTBF uses the observation interval divided by the number of failures, and MTTR uses the mean time from failure detection to service restoration. (found before the rewrite; the slide may have moved)

slide 10 ('Hands‑on: Compute metrics from sample logs'): [other] The lab commands point to a placeholder GitHub organization and provide no repository URL, setup instructions, dependency installation, or verification that the referenced script and data files exist. Fix: Provide the actual accessible repository URL, Python and dependency setup steps, and the expected input-file formats or a command for checking that the lab is ready. (found before the rewrite; the slide may have moved)

findings.message: slide 11 ('Check: Metric definitions'): [clarity] The check asks which metric captures the “worst-case” latency even though no finite percentile captures the absolute worst case. Fix: Ask which metric best captures high-tail user latency and state that p99 estimates the latency below which 99% of observations fall, while the maximum is the observed worst case. (found before the rewrite; the slide may have moved)

slide 13 ('Alerting and anomaly detection on metrics'): [fact] The static threshold example of “error rate > 1%” is presented without a traffic or window qualifier, so it can be misleading for low-volume services or short-lived spikes. Fix: Specify the measurement window and minimum request count, or use an SLO burn-rate threshold that accounts for both rate and traffic. (found before the rewrite; the slide may have moved)

evidence.title: Alerting and anomaly detection on metrics

findings.message: slide 16 ('Using specification‑driven contracts for metrics'): [fact] The CI rule “fails if projected error budget < 10%” is ambiguous about whether 10% means remaining budget or budget consumed, and a projected production error budget is not generally available from ordinary CI tests. Fix: Define the quantity and threshold explicitly, such as “block the release when the projected remaining error budget is below 10%,” and explain how the projection is obtained or use a directly testable SLO assertion. (found before the rewrite; the slide may have moved)
